title: Inhibition of liver X receptor-α-dependent hepatic steatosis by isoliquiritigenin, a licorice antioxidant flavonoid, as mediated by JNK1 inhibition.

a b s t r a c t
Isoliquiritigenin (ILQ), a ﬂavonoid obtained from Glycyrrhizae species, has an antioxidant effect. This study
investigated the potential of ILQ for inhibiting liver X receptor-α (LXRα)-mediated lipogenesis and steatosis
in hepatocytes and its underlying molecular basis. Treatment with ILQ antagonized the ability of an LXRα
agonist (T0901317) to activate sterol regulatory element binding protein-1c (SREBP-1c), thereby repressing
transcription of fatty acid synthase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, ATP-binding cassette transporter-A1, and
stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1. ILQ treatment inhibited activating phosphorylation of JNK1 elicited by palmitate
or TNFα. JNK1, but not JNK2, increased LXRα phosphorylation at serine residues, promoting LXRα activation.
The ability of ILQ to inhibit JNK1 downstream of ASK1–MKK7 led to the repression of T0901317-inducible
LXRα and SREBP-1c activation. In mice fed a high-fat diet, ILQ treatment inhibited hepatic steatosis, as shown
by a decrease in fat accumulation and repression of lipogenic genes. The results of blood biochemistry and
histopathology conﬁrmed attenuation of high-fat diet-induced liver injury by ILQ. Moreover, ILQ inhibited
oxidative stress, as indicated by decreases in thiobarbituric acid-reactive substance formation, iNOS and COX2
induction, and nitrotyrosinylation. Our results demonstrate that ILQ has the ability to repress LXRαdependent hepatic steatosis through JNK1 inhibition and protect hepatocytes from oxidative injury inﬂicted
by fat accumulation.

Liver X receptor-α (LXRα) is a nuclear hormone receptor that
senses and regulates the overall lipid homeostasis [1]. LXRα is
activated by physiological cholesterols (e.g., oxysterol) or chemical
ligands (e.g., T0901317 and GW3965), leading to increases in the
transcriptional activation of target genes including sterol regulatory
element binding protein-1c (SREBP-1c), which is a core regulator of
hepatic lipid metabolism [2]. LXRα enhances SREBP-1c-dependent
lipogenesis through up-regulation of downstream lipogenic genes,
such as fatty acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC),

and cholesterol transporter genes [3]. Furthermore, up-regulated
LXRα-mediated lipogenesis provokes increased inﬂux of
free fatty acid (FFA) to the liver and accumulation of triglyceride
(TG), resulting in development of fatty liver [4]. All together, LXRα
plays a key role in the development and progression of hepatic
steatosis, which may be accompanied by other conditions of
metabolic syndrome (e.g., insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and
hyperlipidemia).
Oxidative stress disturbs the redox homeostasis of the cell and
thereby sometimes causes apoptosis and necrosis when the stress
persists or exceeds the range of the cellular antioxidative capacity [5].
Radical stress induced by high-fat diet (HFD) or proinﬂammatory
cytokines also contributes to the development of nonalcoholic fatty
liver disease (NAFLD), which disturbs the overall normal hepatocyte
physiology and metabolic function [6]. Reactive oxygen species (ROS)
and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) are generated because of upregulated fat accumulation and fatty acid oxidation within hepatocytes, causing oxidative/nitrosative stress in the liver tissue. In
particular, the plasma membranes of hepatocytes are more susceptible to oxidative damage, and the consequent lipid peroxidation of
membranes can provoke cell death [5,6].

With regard to the importance of oxidative stress in NAFLD, recent
studies have indicated that antioxidants might attenuate hepatic
steatosis, steatohepatitis, and even hepatic ﬁbrosis [7–9]. Impaired
ROS scavenging caused by antioxidant deﬁciency, which leads to
progression of NAFLD from simple steatosis to steatohepatitis, might
be the reason for this situation. Furthermore, steatosis-induced lipid
peroxidation can reduce the levels of cellular glutathione and
antioxidant enzymes, thereby increasing the susceptibility of hepatocytes to toxic stimuli [10]. The therapeutic efﬁcacy for treatment of
NAFLD has been examined for several candidates, such as metformin,
N-acetylcysteine, betaine, and vitamin E [7–9]. Although some
promising results were obtained with these agents, the therapeutic
efﬁcacy at reversing hepatic steatosis is limited. Moreover, current
therapeutic interventions for NAFLD are expected to be advanced by
new drugs with different modes of action.
Isoliquiritigenin (ILQ), which belongs to the chalcone and
ﬂavonoid groups characterized by two aromatic rings linked by a
carbon side chain with α,β-unsaturated ketone residues, is obtained
from natural herbs including licorice (Glycyrrhizae radix). Several
studies have investigated the pharmacological effects of ILQ in a
variety of experimental models: ILQ has beneﬁcial effects such as
antioxidant [11,12], anti-inﬂammatory [13–15], and anti-tumor
activities [16–18] and hepatoprotection against chemotherapy-induced toxicity [19]. In a recent study, we found that ILQ has the ability
to protect cells from arachidonic acid plus iron-induced radical stress
and mitochondrial dysfunction [20]. The potential efﬁcacy of ILQ on
the above conditions has been investigated primarily based on its
action as an antioxidative agent. Nonetheless, the effect of ILQ on
hepatic steatosis, which results in oxidative injury of hepatocytes, has
never been explored.
In view of the close link between oxidative stress elicited by fat
accumulation and liver disease progression, this study investigated
the potential of ILQ to inhibit LXRα-mediated lipogenesis and
steatosis in hepatocytes and in vivo models and the underlying
molecular basis. Because c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) physiologically affects fat accumulation [21–23], we explored the role of JNK in
hepatic steatosis and the effect of ILQ on JNK activation. Here, we
report that ILQ has an inhibitory effect on the apoptosis signalregulating kinase-1 (ASK1)–mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase
7 (MKK7)–JNK1 pathway, which contributes to inhibiting LXRαmediated lipogenesis and protecting hepatocytes from oxidative
injury inﬂicted by fat accumulation. Moreover, this study identiﬁed
JNK1 as a novel component that serves as a regulator of LXRα for
hepatic lipogenesis.

Results
Inhibition of LXRα transcriptional activity and lipogenic gene induction
Because LXRα plays a key role in lipid metabolism and contributes
to hepatic steatosis by inducing expression of SREBP-1c, we
determined the effect of ILQ on LXRα activity. First, we examined
the in vitro effect of ILQ treatment on lipogenic gene induction by
T0901317 (T090; an LXRα agonist) in HepG2 cells. ILQ treatment
inhibited T090-mediated LXRα transactivation, as assessed by
CYP7A1–LXRE–luciferase reporter assay (Fig. 1A). Because the LXRα
gene itself contains an LXR response DNA element called LXRE,
agonist activation of LXRα causes its own gene induction [32].
Therefore, we examined the effect of ILQ on mRNA expression of LXRα
using real-time PCR analysis. The mRNA expression of LXRα was
signiﬁcantly increased after treatment with T090 for 12 h; this
induction was inhibited by simultaneous ILQ treatment (Fig. 1B). In
addition, we investigated the expression of SREBP-1c as another
downstream target of LXRα. Consistent with the results shown in
Figs. 1A and B, T090 treatment signiﬁcantly induced SREBP-1c protein
and mRNA levels, which was prevented by ILQ treatment (Fig. 1C).
To more completely understand SREBP-1c activity in cells treated
with T090 and/or ILQ, a FAS reporter gene assay was conducted using
cells transfected with the construct containing the sterol response
element, but not the LXRE, in the −150 bp FAS promoter region.
Exposure of HepG2 cells to T090 increased luciferase activity from the
construct, which was completely diminished by ILQ treatment
(Fig. 2A). The transactivation of genes encoding lipogenic enzymes
is promoted by SREBP-1c, a common transcription factor. In an effort
to clarify the inhibitory effect of ILQ on SREBP-1c-mediated
lipogenesis, the effects of ILQ on the expression of lipogenic genes
were assessed by measuring relative changes in FAS, ACC, ABCA1, and
SCD1 mRNA levels. ILQ treatment signiﬁcantly attenuated the ability
of the LXRα agonist to induce FAS, ACC, ABCA1, and SCD1 (Fig. 2B): a
different data set showed larger decreases in the SCD1 mRNA level.
Our results demonstrate that ILQ has the ability to prevent LXRα–
SREBP-1c-mediated lipogenic gene induction elicited by LXRα agonist
in hepatocytes.
Repression of LXRα-mediated lipogenesis through JNK1 inhibition
HFD feeding causes mitochondrial dysfunction partly because of
increased oxidative stress, which may result from excessive inﬂux of

FFAs [6,33]. In particular, the plasma level of palmitate substantially
increases as a representative saturated FFA in HFD-fed animals [34].
Several lines of evidence indicated that JNK1 might play a role in the
development of obesity, insulin resistance, and steatohepatitis [21–
23]. It has been shown that ILQ has a JNK-inhibitory effect in cells
challenged by stimuli [35,36]. So, we next examined the effect of ILQ
on the phosphorylation of MAPKs in HepG2 cells exposed to
palmitate. ILQ treatment signiﬁcantly attenuated phosphorylation of
JNK1 enhanced by palmitate, but not that of p38 MAPK and ERK
(Fig. 3A). Similarly, ILQ inhibited JNK1 phosphorylation elicited by
TNFα (Fig. 3B), a cytokine induced in the states of obesity, insulin
resistance, and inﬂammation [37,38]. In an effort to ﬁnd the upstream
kinases, the phosphorylation of ASK1, MKK4, and MKK7 was assessed
in cells treated with TNFα. ILQ treatment attenuated MKK7
phosphorylation by TNFα (Fig. 3C). The effect of ILQ on MKK4
phosphorylation was negligible because of weak MKK4 phosphorylation by TNFα (Fig. 3C). ILQ treatment also attenuated ASK1
activating phosphorylation by TNFα (Fig. 3D). In parallel, ILQ
inhibited the ability of TNFα to dissociate thioredoxin from ASK1
(Fig. 3D); it rather increased thioredoxin binding to ASK1.
Chen et al. proposed the possibility that MAPK family members
phosphorylate LXRα although the precise molecular basis has not
been identiﬁed [39]. So, the effect of JNK1/2 overexpression on the
phosphorylation of LXRα was assessed: JNK1 increased LXRα
phosphorylation at serine residues, whereas JNK2 had no effect
(Fig. 4A, left). Moreover, in vitro kinase assay showed that JNK1
directly phosphorylated LXRα (Fig. 4A, right). These results support
the notion that JNK1 plays a major role in regulating LXRα
phosphorylation. The effects of ectopically expressed JNK1 and JNK2
on LXRE reporter activity were also compared: JNK1 increased LXRE–

Effects of ILQ on metabolic parameters and hepatic steatosis
As a continuing effort, we determined the antisteatotic effect of ILQ
in mice fed an HFD. Mice given an HFD for 11 weeks exhibited marked
increases not only in the weights of body, liver, and epididymal fat,
but also in plasma metabolic parameters (Table 1), which is consistent
with our previous report [40]. Treatment of mice with ILQ at the dose
of 10 or 30 mg/kg/day for the last 5 weeks during 11 weeks of HFD
feeding signiﬁcantly decreased body weight and liver weight gains
(Table 1). However, there was no difference in the amount of food
intake among these groups (data not shown). In addition, the
increased levels of glucose and TG in the plasma of HFD-fed mice
were also reversed by ILQ treatment. No signiﬁcant changes were
observed in epididymal fat mass or plasma total cholesterol levels
(Table 1).
Next, we analyzed the hepatic fat accumulation in mice fed an HFD.
HFD feeding for 11 weeks caused severe fat accumulation in the liver
of mice, as indicated by increases in the intensity of oil red O staining
(Fig. 5A) and hepatic TG contents (Fig. 5B). As expected, ILQ treatment
signiﬁcantly attenuated hepatic fat accumulation compared to HFD
alone. Also, the increase in hepatic TG content was antagonized by ILQ
treatment. All of these results are consistent with the changes in
metabolic parameters. Subsequently, the effects of ILQ treatment on
the levels of lipogenic gene transcripts were determined in the liver of
HFD-fed mice. In parallel with the inhibition of hepatic fat accumulation by ILQ, the increased mRNA levels of lipogenic genes encoding
LXRα, SREBP-1c, FAS, ACC, and SCD1 were all repressed by ILQ
treatment (Fig. 5C). Overall, ILQ had a bona ﬁde antisteatotic effect in
the liver of HFD-fed mice, which was accompanied by the inhibition of
LXRα and SREBP-1c expression.
Effect of ILQ on HFD-induced oxidative injury
To test whether ILQ has an antioxidant effect in mice fed an HFD,
we measured formation of TBARS, an index of lipid peroxidation, in
the liver tissue (Fig. 6A). As expected, HFD feeding enhanced TBARS
formation in the liver homogenates, which was drastically prevented
by ILQ treatment (10 mg/kg/day). Moreover, HFD feeding induced
the expression of hepatic iNOS and COX2, pro-oxidant enzymes,

which was also abrogated by ILQ treatment (Fig. 6B). Immunohistochemical analysis conﬁrmed the inhibitory effect of ILQ on HFDinduced oxidative injury. Nitrotyrosine is a well-characterized
hallmark of protein oxidation induced by RNS. Consistent with the
above results, nitrotyrosinylation was clearly increased in the liver
tissue of mice fed an HFD (Fig. 6C). The intensity of staining was
stronger around the pericentral area. ILQ treatment (10 mg/kg/day)
attenuated the intensity of nitrotyrosine staining increased by HFD

accompanied by increases in TBARS formation, pro-oxidant enzyme
induction, and protein nitration, all of which were antagonized by
ILQ treatment.
In an effort to assess the effect of ILQ on hepatocyte injury, we further
determined whether ILQ is capable of protecting the liver from HFDinduced liver injury. The blood biochemical analysis showed that ALT
activity, which is located speciﬁcally in the liver, was increased in mice fed
an HFD for 11 weeks, whereas simultaneous ILQ treatment at the dose of
10 mg/kg/day during the last 5 weeks of the diet feeding inhibited the
increase in plasma ALT activity (Fig. 7A). By histopathological observation,
HFD feeding induced the formation of large cytoplasmic lipid droplets and
hepatocyte death, which were all ameliorated by ILQ treatment (10 mg/
kg/day; Fig. 7B). These results demonstrate that ILQ inhibits hepatic fat
accumulation, thereby protecting the liver from HFD-induced oxidative
stress and hepatic injury.
To conﬁrm the inhibitory effect of ILQ on JNK1 in vivo, we ﬁnally
examined the effects of ILQ on the phosphorylation of JNK1 in the liver
of HFD-fed mice. HFD feeding conspicuously increased JNK1 phosphorylation. Consistent with the results of the cell model experiment,
ILQ treatment abrogated the phosphorylation of JNK1 enhanced by
HFD feeding (Fig. 8A). All of these results demonstrate that ILQ has an
inhibitory effect on hepatic steatosis, through the inhibition of ASK1–
MKK7–JNK1 activation elicited by excess fat.
Discussion
Licorice (G. radix) products have been consumed on a large scale
and used as remedies worldwide. It has been shown that the
ﬂavonoids obtained from licorice have diverse biological activities.
In particular, ILQ has antioxidant, anti-inﬂammatory, and anti-tumor
effects [11–19]. In addition, treatment with ILQ alters the conformation of Kelch-like ECH-associated protein-1 by alkylating speciﬁc
cysteine residues, resulting in NF-E2-related factor-2 activation
[41,42], which may be associated with the antioxidative and
cytoprotective effects of ILQ. Also, ILQ increased heme oxygenase-1
expression and inhibited the production of proinﬂammatory cytokines in LPS-stimulated macrophages [15]. Moreover, ILQ inhibited
mitochondrial dysfunction caused by iron-catalyzed severe oxidative
stress [20]. It effectively decreases mitochondrial superoxide generation as well as cellular hydrogen peroxide production induced by
arachidonic acid plus iron [20]. Thus, ILQ is capable of protecting cells
from severe oxidative stress. Nonetheless, the agent does not have a

LXRα, which is highly expressed in the liver, serves as a nuclear
sensor for cholesterol, thereby regulating lipid homeostasis [1]. LXRα
forms a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor for full transactivation and binds to LXREs in the promoter region of LXRα itself and
SREBP-1c, leading to increased expression of SREBP-1c [44]. In this
study, ILQ inhibited LXRα-mediated SREBP-1c activation and SREBP1c-dependent lipogenic gene induction in an in vitro model, as
evidenced by reporter gene assay, real-time PCR assay, and immunoblotting for downstream targets of LXRα–SREBP-1c. Consistent with
the results of the in vitro study, ILQ treatment considerably
suppressed fat accumulation and de novo lipid synthesis in the liver
of mice fed an HFD. Our observation that ILQ effectively prevented the
increases in mRNA levels of LXRα, SREBP-1c, and downstream
lipogenic genes and decreased hepatic TG content in an HFD-fed
animal model strongly supports antilipogenic efﬁcacy. Moreover,
blood glucose and TG contents were also diminished in HFD-fed mice
treated with ILQ. Collectively, ILQ has a bona ﬁde antisteatotic effect in
the liver, as strengthened by both in vitro and in vivo results.
JNK may serve as a regulator in the development of obesity and
insulin resistance [21–23]; JNK plays a role in both systemic and

hepatic insulin resistance through serine phosphorylation of the IRS1
and IRS2, leading to down-modulation of tyrosine phosphorylation of
these molecules required for normal insulin signaling [21–23,45].
Also, JNK activation by stimuli such as oxidative stress, obesityinduced inﬂammation, and increase in FFA inﬂux causes insulin
resistance and steatosis in the liver [23,45]. Most cells, including
hepatocytes, express two forms of JNK, Jnk1 and Jnk2, which are
alternatively spliced to yield α and β forms of both p54 and p46
proteins [21,22]. Among these, JNK1 promoted the development of
steatohepatitis in mice fed a methionine- and choline-deﬁcient diet,
whereas JNK2 failed to do so [22]. In another study, both JNK1 and
JNK2 mediated insulin resistance induced by HFD feeding, but had
different roles in pathogenesis; JNK1 promoted steatosis and
hepatitis, whereas JNK2 regulated insulin signaling independent of
hepatic steatosis [21]. Hence, JNK1 seemed to be important in the
progression of NAFLD, making itself an attractive target for treating
NAFLD.
Posttranslational modiﬁcations may be regulatory mechanisms for
diverse nuclear receptors. Here, we found that either palmitate or
TNFα, whose content in plasma was elevated in the states of hepatic
steatosis and insulin resistance [34,37,38], activates JNK1. Our
observation showing JNK1 activation by these treatments suggests
the close link between JNK1 and lipogenesis. In this study, JNK1 was
identiﬁed as a novel upstream regulator for hepatic LXRα activation
and LXRα-dependent lipogenesis. Our hypothesis is supported by the
ﬁnding that either DN-JNK1 transfection or JNK inhibitor treatment

Our ﬁnding that DN-JNK1 inhibited T090-induced LXRE reporter
activity and SREBP-1c induction suggests that JNK1 is necessary for
LXRα activation. This contention is further strengthened by the
observation that enforced JNK1 expression not only promoted LXRE–

Another important ﬁnding of this study is that ILQ antagonizes the
activation of JNK1 elicited by palmitate or TNFα treatment in a cell
model. The lack of changes in p38 MAPK and ERK supports its speciﬁc
effect. Moreover, the inhibitory effect of ILQ on JNK1 was veriﬁed by
immunoblotting for phosphorylated JNK1 in liver homogenates.
Consistent with the concept that JNK1 promotes LXRα-mediated
lipogenesis, our observation indicates that ILQ's inhibition of JNK1
contributes to the repression of LXRα and LXRα-dependent gene
induction. Likewise, ILQ reversed LXRα-mediated gene induction
elicited by JNK1 overexpression. The link between the JNK1 pathway
and LXRα-mediated hepatic lipogenesis was further strengthened by
the ectopically expressed JNK1's reversal of the ability of ILQ to inhibit

LXRα-mediated SREBP-1c induction. Our results indicated that ILQ
suppressed JNK1 by inhibiting ASK1–MKK7 activation. Overall, the
inhibition of ASK1–MKK7–JNK1 by ILQ may account for its inhibitory
effect on hepatic lipogenesis (Fig. 8B). In the previous study, we
identiﬁed two other kinases that act on LXRα; S6K1 phosphorylated
LXRα at serine residues to increase its gene transactivation, whereas
AMPK phosphorylated LXRα at threonine residues, which resulted in
inactivation of LXRα [28]. Our supplementary study showed that
either DN-AMPK transfection or compound C (an AMPK inhibitor)
treatment failed to reverse the repression of LXRα-dependent gene
induction by ILQ (data not shown), raising the possibility that the
inhibition of the ASK1–MM7–JNK1 pathway by ILQ prevails over
AMPK–S6K1-dependent regulation of LXRα.
Oxidative stress promotes the progression of various diseases by
altering intracellular redox homeostasis, mainly through generating
ROS/RNS. Several studies have investigated the therapeutic efﬁcacy of
antioxidants in preventing hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis
[7,9,40]. Once hepatic steatosis has developed upon HFD feeding,
accumulation of FFAs causes increased fatty acid oxidation and this
status itself becomes toxic (i.e., lipotoxicity) [5]. Thus, HFD feeding
provokes oxidative stress in the liver, priming hepatocellular injury
through mitochondrial dysfunction, lysosomal dysregulation, and
inﬂammatory response [5]. In the “two-hit” model, increased ROS
production caused by increased hepatic fat accumulation plays a key
role as the second hit in inducing nonalcoholic steatohepatitis [8,46].
In this study, we observed enhanced oxidative/nitrosative stress in
the liver of mice fed an HFD, as evidenced by increased TBARS
formation, iNOS and COX2 induction, and nitrotyrosinylation, which
were all prevented by ILQ. In addition, the level of plasma ALT, which
mainly localizes within hepatocytes, was also increased upon HFD
feeding, and this was also antagonized by ILQ treatment. All of these
results support the antisteatotic and antioxidant effects of ILQ.
Among the alterations in physiological responses upon HFD
feeding, JNK1 activation is most responsible for HFD-induced
oxidative stress and hepatic steatosis [21–23,47]. Hence, JNK1
inhibition by ILQ would contribute to not only the inhibition of
LXRα-dependent hepatic steatosis, but also the antioxidative effect in
the liver of HFD-fed mice (Fig. 8B). ILQ has the ability to protect cells
from arachidonic acid plus iron-induced H2O2 production and
mitochondrial dysfunction, which was mediated in part by AMPK
activation leading to inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β [20]. So, ILQ
has a direct mitochondrial protective effect, which depends on its
AMPK activation. Hence, the beneﬁcial effects of ILQ on hepatic
steatosis may be multivalent as a consequence of direct mitochondrial
protection as well as the inhibition of LXRα-mediated lipogenesis and
radical stress. After oral administration, ILQ is metabolized by phase I
and phase II enzymes, which include cytochrome P450s and UDPglucuronosyltransferases in the intestine and liver [48,49]. In animal
experiments, ILQ glucuronide conjugates were found in plasma,
which might also have pharmacological activities [50].
In conclusion, the results of this study demonstrate that ILQ has
beneﬁcial efﬁcacy in treating hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis by
inhibiting lipogenesis and fat-induced oxidative injury. Furthermore,
JNK1 was identiﬁed as a novel upstream component that regulates
LXRα activity. Our ﬁnding that ILQ inhibits LXRα-mediated lipogenesis through ASK1–MKK7–JNK1 inhibition may be informative not
only in elucidating JNK1 as an attractive target, but also in
demonstrating the potential use of ILQ as a unique ﬂavonoid for the
treatment of hepatic steatosis and steatohepatitis.
